entry.title: How to destroy thorns in Crimson Desert
entry.summary:
There's a fair bit of exploration to do in Crimson Desert, and sometimes, you'll come across thorns that will block your path (probably to treasures beyond our imagination). It's best to harness fire if you want to get rid of thorns, and there are a few ways to do that.
How to use fire to destroy thorns in Crimson Desert
The easiest way to destroy thorns in Crimson Desert is to deal fire damage with either fire arrows or the Blinding Flash skill. Let's cover the skill first.
Step one is to equip a sword.
Press and hold the Ctrl and LMB at the same time.
You can now use the skill by releasing and holding the Ctrl button.
If you're on a console, you can engage the activated stance by pressing and holding the RB/R1 and LB/L1 buttons.
Release RB/R1 and then hold it again to release flash.
Image via Pearl Abyss
Doing so will focus an intense beam of light on the thorns and set them on fire. Wait for a few seconds, and the vines will disappear. You'll unlock Blinding Flash pretty early in the game. It's part of an opening puzzle that has to be solved to open a locked door.
If you're not using a sword, you use fire arrows.
First, you have to find standard wooden arrows, which are relatively easy to find.
Next, find a source of fire.
Draw the bow, and touch the arrow's tip with the fire. This will set the arrow ablaze.
Aim at the thorns to shoot the arrow, and this will clear your path.
I prefer using Blinding Flash, as you might not always have a source of fire readily available while you're out and about.

entry.title: How to summon your companions in Crimson Desert
entry.summary:
Crimson Desert might be a single-player experience at heart, but you don't need to play alone. There are pet companions you can find on your adventures who will accompany you wherever you go. But you can also get two additional companion characters in the form of Damaine and Oongka.
While you can play as them if you want, you can also have them as a companion to join you on your adventure.
How to use companions in Crimson Desert
The first step is to unlock Damaine and Oongka, which can be done as you complete the main campaign. If you're a beginner, it will take some time for you to unlock both. Once you unlock them, both Damaine and Oongka will be permanently available for you to pick from.
Image via Pearl Abyss
But you can only play as one character at any given time. If you switch from Kliff to, let's say, Damaine, the other character will be controlled by the AI. To summon characters as companions, open the character radial menu. Select the companion and then summon them.
You'll need to wait slightly for them to arrive, and once they do, they will follow you wherever you go. Having a companion is extremely useful since they can help you to take down enemies. However, they won't join you in boss fights, which need to be done on your own. They will also be unable to solve any puzzles for you, which also have to be done on your own.
That said, having someone to aid you in general combat is always helpful. You can also have your own pets that can act as additional companions. They won't help you in combat, but they will help you with loot collection, which saves a lot of time and energy.

entry.title: Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus review: another skippable CPU series
entry.summary: Regardless of whether Intel would say it out loud, the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and Core Ultra 5 250K Plus both represent an attempt to right the wrongs of the original Arrow Lake/Core Ultra 200S family. That bundle of chips was, necessarily, more power-efficient and cooler-running than the hotheaded 14th Gen models before them, though this came at the cost of hamstrung gaming performance. Rarely a desirable quality in a gaming CPU, that. These two Core Ultra 200S Plus (or Arrow Lake Refresh) processors do, in comparison, achieve some appeal. They’re inexpensive and excellent multitaskers, and while they do still have efficiency on their silicon brains, Intel have looked to bump game speeds back up by rejigging their innards into a less latency-prone layout. Alas, it’s not enough. Not only are Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and Core Ultra 5 250K Plus slower in games than AMD’s best chips, they once again fail to convincingly outpace Intel’s own back catalogue – the 2023 vintage 14th gen processors, included. entry.title: How to get Bismuth in Crimson Desert
entry.summary:
Bismuth is a difficult resource to get in Crimson Desert, and you'll need to look in specific locations to find some. When you're around the material, you'll be able to identify it from its signature silver base and shimmer.
Thanks to its mystical power, you can't mine Bismuth with ordinary tools. This guide will help you find Bismuth and mine it as much as you need.
Table of contents How to mine Bismuth in Crimson Desert Best Bismuth farm location in Crimson Desert
How to mine Bismuth in Crimson Desert
While most of the mining in Crimson Desert is done with the pickaxe, it won't work on Bismuth. You'll first need to use Lightning Surge to break the magic barrier that surrounds Bismuth deposits. You won't be able to mine as long as the barrier is active.
Image via Pearl Abyss
Naturally, you'll need Lightning at level 1 before you head to a location where you can find Bismuth (more on that later). Press RT+B/RB+Circle to generate an electric field. Release it to bring down the barrier. To mine Bismuth, you need to hit the spot where the electric field hits.
Best Bismuth farm location in Crimson Desert
Screenshot and remix by Destructoid
There are several locations in Crimson Desert, but the best one can be found near the Scholastone Institute. Go southwest from Hernand City, and you'll find the Institute on the map. The ore is found along the mountain cliffs near a waterfall.
As an alternative, you can also look to find Bismuth in the peaks of Everfrost. Usually, you'll find plenty of Bismuth Ore in the locations mentioned above. Hence, make sure to have enough space in your inventory so that you can carry as much ore as required.
The post How to get Bismuth in Crimson Desert appeared first on Destructoid.

entry.title: Systemd umožní ověřování věku uživatelů
entry.summary:
Projekt systemd schválil kontroverzní pull request, který do JSON záznamů uživatelů přidává nové pole 'birthDate', datum narození, tedy údaj vyžadovaný zákony o ověřování věku v Kalifornii, Coloradu a Brazílii. Jiný pull request, který tuto změnu napravoval, byl správcem projektu Lennartem Poetteringem zamítnut s následujícím zdůvodněním:
'Jedná se o volitelné pole v JSON userdb objektu, nejedná se o žádný modul pro správu pravidel (not a policy engine) ani o API pro aplikace. Toto pole pouze definujeme, aby bylo standardizované pro případ, že by tam někdo chtěl ukládat datum, ale je zcela volitelné. Proto prosím přesuňte svou diskuzi jinam, nepochopili jste, jakou roli zde systém systemd hraje - nevymáhá žádné pravidla, jejich nastavení ponechává na jiných částech systému. A promiňte, ale tyto debaty mě tady opravdu nezajímají. Tohle není správné místo pro takové věci, tak je sem prosím nezatahujte. Děkuji.'

entry.title: Far Cry's open world takes on new significance when you consider the etymology of "explore"
entry.summary:
During a random dictionary delve last week I learned that "explore" once meant to cry out. It comes from an old Latin word formed from the prefix "ex-", describing outwardness, and "plorare", meaning to cry or weep. Compare "implore" - to beg, cry for something - and "deplore" - to berate, 'cry of' something or somebody.
The OED explains ("ex + "planō", meaning to level off, flatten for understanding) that "explore" may originally have referred to hunters, shouting to scare up animals lurking in the area around them. Exploration was always somewhat predatory, then, perhaps a little anguished. I have to admit, I got misty-eyed on discovering all this, thinking about how this word I've written a million times in videogame reviews is a kind of silenced wail.

entry.title: "You're not doing parkour off a roof, but the principles were the same": How the makers of Firewatch pulled from Mirror's Edge, Far Cry 2, and Bioshock to tell a new kind of story in a walking simulator
entry.summary: In May 2014, the small team at Campo Santo were still in the early days of making Firewatch, a first-person narrative exploration game – you can call it a walking simulator, they do, and with no disparagement. The developers assembled at their San Francisco offices, some came from nearby, others from as far away as Vancouver, Canada and Winchester in the UK. They loaded up cars with beer, board games, and tents, and drove the several hours to Yosemite National Park, where, as one of Campo Santo's founders Nels Anderson puts it, "We went camping in the goddamn woods." While Firewatch was always due to be set more than 500 miles away in Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, the team wanted to get deep into a forest and find the feeling of being surrounded and overwhelmed by nature. "All of us would say we were highly informed by that trip," Chris Remo says. He remembers thinking "In a year and a half, this is the thing we will have hopefully captured some little part of."
